L94: Formally, we propose MicroEP, a novel EP strategy that leverages token scheduling for fine-grained load balancing across GPUs. MicroEP optimizes load balancing from two perspectives: (1) From a short-term perspective, MicroEP schedules tokens within every micro-batch using linear programming to minimize the maximum GPU loads (§cite16†5.1 ).
L95: To optimize system efficiency, MicroEP reduces the communication volume through locality-aware routing (§cite17†5.2 ) and minimizes the scheduling latency through efficient overlapping (§cite19†5.4 ). (2) From a long-term perspective, MicroEP tailors expert placement to optimize the token scheduling performance and mitigate coarse-grained imbalances. Based on our theoretical analysis, MicroEP adopts multiple expert placement strategies (§cite22†6.2 -cite23†6.3 ) and an adaptive replacement mechanism (§cite24†6.4 ).
L180: An example. Surprisingly, MicroEP can almost always achieve perfect load balance among GPUs, unless the expert load distribution is extremely skewed (as shown in §cite28†7.3 ). We can intuitively learn how MicroEP achieves such good performance from the example in Figure cite100†3(c) . Since expert 3 is heavily loaded, it places 8 tokens on GPU 3, preventing expert 0 from placing any token on the same GPU. Fortunately, expert 0 can place all its 4 tokens on GPU 0.
L181: Similarly, expert 2 also “shifts” some load from GPU 2 to GPU 1, while expert 1 shifts some load from GPU 1 to GPU 0. Consequently, the computational burden of heavily loaded experts is effectively distributed across the entire MicroEP group.
L182: ## 5. Token Scheduling
L183: Token scheduling is the core of MicroEP for fine-grained load balancing. The scheduling algorithm runs in two steps: The first step is to distribute expert loads among their replicas, balancing GPU loads (§cite16†5.1 ). The second step is to route tokens to specific expert replicas, enforcing the calculated replica loads (§cite17†5.2 ). Then, we discuss where and when to launch the scheduling in §cite18†5.3 and §cite19†5.4 . Finally, we discuss some additional scheduling optimizations in Appendix cite36†A .
L184: ### 5.1. Determining Replica Loads
L185: 
L186: We aim to balance GPU loads through optimal distribution of expert loads among their replicas. We formulate the load balancing problem as an optimization problem.

Let $E$ represent the set of all experts, $G_{MicroEP}$ represent the set of GPUs in the concerned MicroEP group, and $G_{EDP}^{e}$ represent the set of GPUs in the EDP group of expert $e$. Since we currently focus on a single MicroEP group, we assume that $G_{EDP}^{e}\subseteq G_{MicroEP},\forall e\in E$.

L204: Variables. The variables are $\{x_{e}^{g}:e\in E,g\in G_{EDP}^{e}\}$, where $x_{e}^{g}$ is the replica load of expert $e$ on GPU $g$.
L205: 
L206:   * •
L207: Constraints. Let $load_{e}(e\in E)$ denote the total load (number of tokens) of expert $e$ in the concerned MicroEP group. A valid distribution must ensure that each expert distributes its total load across its replicas.

L211: Objective. Due to synchronization requirements for all-to-all communication before and after expert computation, the GPU with the highest load becomes the performance bottleneck. Therefore, we should minimize the maximum GPU load across the MicroEP group.
L212: We formulate the optimization problem as follows.
L213: 
L214: (1)  |  | $\displaystyle\text{minimize}$  | $\displaystyle\max\limits_{g\in G_{MicroEP}}\left\{\sum\limits_{e\in E:g\in G_{EDP}^{e}}x_{e}^{g}\right\},$  |
L215:  | $\displaystyle\text{subject to}$  | $\displaystyle\sum\limits_{g\in G_{EDP}^{e}}x_{e}^{g}=load_{e},\quad\forall e\in E,$  |
L216:  |  | $\displaystyle x_{e}^{g}\geq 0,\quad\forall e\in E,g\in G_{EDP}^{e}.$  |
L217: Problem cite102†1 is a linear programming problem (LPP), which can be efficiently solved in polynomial time relative to the number of GPUs and experts. The number of variables is $O(|E|d)$, and the number of constraints is $O(|E|+|G_{MicroEP}|)$. Given its modest scale, we solve this LPP using a single CPU thread with the HiGHs solver (cite103†Huangfu and Hall, 2018 ). GPU acceleration or multi-threading would not yield significant performance benefits for this scale of optimization.

L258: ### 5.3. Distributed Scheduling across Devices
L259: 
L260: As described in §cite16†5.1 and §cite17†5.2 , the scheduling algorithm requires the global load information ($input_{e}^{g}$) across the entire MicroEP group as input. This raises the question of where to place the scheduler.
L261: We consider two candidate locations for the scheduler: centralized on one device or distributed across all devices. A centralized scheduler needs to gather load information from all devices, perform the scheduling, and scatter the results. Alternatively, distributed schedulers require all devices to perform an all-gather operation to collect global load information and execute the scheduling algorithm independently.
L262: We choose the distributed approach for better scalability because it requires only one communication operation compared to two operations in the centralized approach. Since the load information is small, the primary performance factor is latency rather than throughput, making fewer communication operations advantageous.
L263: Notably, the distributed scheduling maintains consistency because MicroEP’s scheduling algorithm is deterministic—all devices use identical inputs, follow identical algorithms, and produce identical results.
L374: We conducted an ablation study to evaluate three optimizations in MicroMoE: (1) warm solving in §cite16†5.1 , (2) locality-aware routing in §cite17†5.2 , and (3) overlapping in §cite19†5.4 . All these optimizations aim to reduce the dispatch time. As shown in Figure cite122†11 , both warm solving and overlapping reduce scheduling time, while locality-aware routing reduces all-to-all communication time.
L375: With the combination of optimizations, MicroMoE introduces only 0.4 ms additional dispatch time compared to vanilla Megatron-LM. This modest overhead is substantially outweighed by the reduced computation time, ensuring the overall system efficiency of MicroMoE.

L94: Formally, we propose MicroEP, a novel EP strategy that leverages token scheduling for fine-grained load balancing across GPUs. MicroEP optimizes load balancing from two perspectives: (1) From a short-term perspective, MicroEP schedules tokens within every micro-batch using linear programming to minimize the maximum GPU loads (§cite16†5.1 ).
L95: To optimize system efficiency, MicroEP reduces the communication volume through locality-aware routing (§cite17†5.2 ) and minimizes the scheduling latency through efficient overlapping (§cite19†5.4 ). (2) From a long-term perspective, MicroEP tailors expert placement to optimize the token scheduling performance and mitigate coarse-grained imbalances. Based on our theoretical analysis, MicroEP adopts multiple expert placement strategies (§cite22†6.2 -cite23†6.3 ) and an adaptive replacement mechanism (§cite24†6.4 ).
L96: These optimizations enable MicroEP to maintain complete load balance under dynamic and highly skewed expert loads.
L97: Based on MicroEP, we design MicroMoE, an efficient distributed MoE training system. We implement MicroMoE upon Megatron-LM (cite83†Shoeybi et al., 2020 ) and evaluate its load balancing performance. Experimental results show that MicroMoE achieves up to 47.6% improvement on end-to-end throughput compared with Megatron-LM and maintains complete load balance even under highly imbalanced workloads.
